analysis.one_liner: Delays Medicare drug price negotiation for pill medicines from 7 years after approval to 11.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without a hearing or vote in two House committees since its February 2025 introduction, despite 68 cosponsors — 64 Republicans and 4 Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare now sets prices for some of the most expensive brand-name drugs. Under current law, a typical pill (a small-molecule drug) becomes open to Medicare price negotiation 7 years after approval, while biologic drugs (usually injections or infusions) wait 11 years. This bill would extend the pill waiting period to 11 years, and apply the change retroactively — meaning some drugs already slated for negotiation could get four more years before Medicare can bargain their prices down.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers of small-molecule drugs gain roughly four extra years of sales at unregulated list prices before Medicare can negotiate. Drugs already chosen for negotiation could see that delayed by the bill's retroactive effective date.

how_it_helps.text: It would give small-molecule drugs the same 11-year waiting period before Medicare negotiation that biologics already have, instead of 7 years.

The change applies retroactively, taking effect as if it were part of the original 2022 law that created the negotiation program — which could pull drugs already scheduled for negotiation out of the process.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers bear the cost: price negotiation on pill medicines would start up to four years later, adding years of payments at unregulated prices for drugs already on Medicare's list.

drawbacks.text: Delaying negotiation by four years means Medicare and its beneficiaries keep paying higher, unregulated prices on affected drugs for years longer than current law allows.
The retroactive effective date could unwind drug selections already made under the negotiation program, reversing price reductions already in motion.

Supporters' best-faith case is that the shorter 7-year window for pills — which the industry calls a 'pill penalty' — discourages companies from developing new small-molecule medicines, which patients often prefer because they can be taken at home; this bill would remove that imbalance. Critics respond that the way to fix that is prospectively, not by retroactively delaying savings on drugs already on the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated rationale — treating pills and biologics the same so drug companies don't steer away from making new pills — is a real policy debate. But this bill's direct effect is to postpone Medicare's price negotiation on pill drugs by four years, retroactively, which shifts billions in costs onto seniors and taxpayers in exchange for an investment incentive that is speculative and could have been addressed without touching drugs already in the pipeline.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in February 2025 and neither has scheduled it for a hearing, a markup, or a vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Gregory Murphy introduced the bill on February 21, 2025, joined by Representatives Davis of North Carolina and Hudson.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
The bill requires small-molecule drugs to have 11 years of market approval — up from 7 — before Medicare can negotiate their price, and the change applies retroactively.
It attracted 68 cosponsors: 64 of 223 House Republicans and 4 of 216 House Democrats.
No further action appears in the record since the February 2025 referrals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, seniors and taxpayers are better off than they would be under the bill, since Medicare's current negotiation timelines remain intact while the bill sits in committee; brand-name drug makers avoid losing nothing but gain nothing yet either.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lengthen the small-molecule negotiation waiting period to 11 years, retroactively.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill in February 2025; the committee has taken no further action since.

sides.party_line_note: Support skews heavily Republican: 64 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored versus 4 of 216 House Democrats, and no chamber vote has occurred.

industries.note: The bill gives their pill drugs four extra years before Medicare can negotiate prices, retroactively — years of sales at unregulated list prices paid for by Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Its interest in this bill runs directly against the public's interest in lower drug prices.

Biologics' own 11-year negotiation timeline would not change. But equalizing the two timelines would remove the current rule that steers manufacturers toward biologics (which get four extra years of unregulated pricing under current law), so the bill takes away a relative planning advantage they now hold.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no committee action since its February 2025 referrals. Bills at this stage with limited Democratic support and no committee movement typically die when the Congress ends, unless a similar provision is attached to a larger health or Medicare package.
